explanation: Fires on whitespace, newlines, separator dashes and other structural tokens at the boundary between a document header and its body. Typical spots: after court-opinion captions ('Before X, Y, Circuit Judges.', reporter citations like '37 F.3d 477' followed by a newline), after a wire-story dateline ('(UPI) --'), at a code body's opening indentation, and at Markdown section anchors '{#'. Ordinary mid-sentence words fire only weakly and sporadically.

Fires on the token that completes a locative or part-whole noun phrase, often a preposition like 'in' or 'of' that links an entity to its container ('part of', 'state of', 'fire in', 'district', 'passed in'). Also fires on assorted code-argument tokens and name-suffix tokens. The pattern is loose and has no single clear trigger.

Fires inside opaque alphanumeric identifiers: hex color codes, UUID hyphens, postcode digits, hex opcodes, and prefix fragments of CamelCase class names or chemical names (e.g. 'carb-ony-l'). It responds to sub-word pieces in the middle of non-word strings, not to natural-language words.

Fires on the first sub-word fragment of a longer word that the tokenizer splits, mainly at a word start after a space: 'extr' in extracellular/extraintestinal, 'Kar' in Karavelas/Karloff, 'Nar', 'Str', 'tr', 'par'. Strongest on 'extr-' prefixes in biomedical text and on the opening fragments of surnames.

Fires on metadata field keys and markup attribute names in structured headers. Strongest on 'author' at the start of a YAML front-matter line after an abstract, then 'title', 'address', 'Date', '@license', 'page_title', 'figure' in \captionof, and the punctuation of shortcode or markdown attributes. Ordinary prose does not fire.

Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word or name that continues in the next token, especially capitalised name starts ('P'ietro, 'B'uhari, 'B'ND, 'S'ANTA, 'R'iga) and prefixes such as 'r'ife, 'ob'eylines, 'babys'at and 'trans'national. It also fires on some punctuation in French text. It mostly follows the 'incomplete word fragment' pattern but is noisy.

Fires on a word-initial fragment of a multi-token word, often a proper noun or foreign-language word ('Be'itragszentrale, 'Min'ke, 'con'creto, 'Pal'occi, 'Be'ale, 'Mon'mouthshire), and especially in non-English text (German, Portuguese, French, Romanian). It anticipates how the word continues. Function words fire only weakly.

Fires on a mixed bag of tokens: word pieces inside medical or anatomical terms ('infer'ot'emporal', 'atr'io'ventricular', 'interle'uk'in'), list separators and conjunctions between coordinated items ('Numbers,', 'Intra- and'), Japanese noun suffixes, and some modal or copula verbs. No single shared feature is evident.

Fires on words in requests for supporting material or help, the thing that should be supplied or attached: 'add screenshots', 'screen shot', 'error details', 'send a link', 'so we can send you a copy', 'let me know', 'additional facts are needed'. Common in bug-report templates, Q&A help posts and license boilerplate.

Fires on function words and punctuation in casual narrative or informal prose that begin a predicate or noun phrase: articles 'a'/'the', copulas 'is', possessive ''s', 'like', 'for', and an opening parenthesis before an abbreviation or aside. It seems to track a general position-in-sentence or style feature rather than any particular lexical item, so it is hard to predict.

Fires on assorted tokens in code and technical text: '.com' in Go 'github.com' imports, 'memory' in C++ '#include <memory>', 'cap' in LaTeX set notation, and mid-word pieces of names and foreign words (HERNAN'DE'Z, Med'line', Jyvä'sk'ylä). The examples share no clear concept beyond these clusters.

Fires on the letters of an abbreviation being defined inside parentheses right after its spelled-out form ('end stage renal failure (ES[RD])', '(C[JR])', '(DRAM)', '(AMI)'), usually on the token after the first letter. Weaker activity comes from short name or word fragments right after a capital letter ('M'uld'row', 'D'ipt'era').

Fires on the 'import' keyword (Java/Kotlin) or 'use' keyword (PHP) at the start of a line in a source file's import block after the package/namespace declaration, strongest when it follows earlier import lines. Weak, sporadic offshoots appear on mid-word fragments and on broken multi-byte CJK characters.

Fires on the hyphen between two years in copyright notices ('Copyright (C) 1997-1998', '2016-2020'), and more generally on range dashes between numbers. Weaker, scattered offshoots appear on conversational retorts ('You kidding?', 'Fear not') and on code-comment tokens.
